title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (1 of 7)
hook: a boy watches his father give away worn-out cows, and asks one question too many
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Last week, tadvana, the dear one: the victory was never theirs, it was Brahman's. Your line was the one behind the ear. Did you thank someone whose help you didn't see? Day two hundred forty-six.

A charity drive at a big house. The owner is making a show of generosity, and his servants lead the gifts out one by one. But the kid in the doorway notices something. The gifts are the old stuff. Cows that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk. Cows that will never calf again. Everyone else nods politely. The boy can't. This is how the Katha Upanishad begins: a boy named Nachiketa, a father's careless gift, and, before long, Death.
screen: `A SHOW OF GENEROSITY.` → `THE OLD COWS.` → `THE BOY IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: The father is called Vajashravasa, and he's performing a sacrifice where you're meant to give away everything you own. But the cows he gives are worn out. The text says it bluntly: they've drunk their water, eaten their grass, been milked dry, and will bear no more. Joyless worlds, it says, await the one who gives gifts like these. Then: shraddha entered the boy. Shraddha is faith, trust, a kind of deep seriousness. You met it in the Gita. It enters Nachiketa, still a child, and he goes to his father. Father, to whom will you give me? Because if the sacrifice means giving everything, then the son belongs on the list. It's a real question and a sharp one. The father doesn't answer. Nachiketa asks a second time. Then a third. And the father, angry, the way a parent can when a child sees through them in front of others, snaps: I give you to Death. To Yama. Stop there. It's an ancient story, and it's also a very modern one. A parent says something in anger they can't take back. A child takes them at their word. Nachiketa doesn't run and hide. He thinks it through: I go first among many, in the middle of many. What will Yama do with me? He sees that all people ripen and fall like grain, and rise again like grain. And he goes. This week is the Katha, and its word is the two paths. We'll reach them on day three. It starts with a boy who couldn't pretend old cows were a gift.
screen: `THE WORN-OUT COWS.` · `SHRADDHA ENTERED THE BOY.` · `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` · `I GIVE YOU TO DEATH.` · then, large: `NACHIKETA AND DEATH.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of something you've given lately: time, money, attention, help. Be honest, gently. Was it a real gift, or a worn-out one: the leftover hour, the distracted ear, the thing you didn't want anyway? No blame. Just notice. Then think of one real thing you could give this week, something that would cost you a little. Hold it. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Nachiketa. A boy whose father, angry, said: I give you to Death. Shraddha, faith, had entered him, and he went to Yama's house without fear.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, when you give something, give the real thing, not the leftover. Day two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Hindus tell the Katha's story of Nachiketa to children and also study it closely; Vedanta teachers, Shankara among them, wrote commentaries on it.

fork.setup: you're a child watching your father give away worthless cows as if they were a great gift. what do you do?
options: say nothing; it's not your place.
ask him: to whom will you give me?
fork.reveal: Nachiketa asks, three times. his father snaps: to Death I give you. and the boy goes.

original.note: Sanskrit: Nachiketa (stem nachiketas), the boy at the heart of the Katha.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a story about a cruel father.
what it means: it starts with a false gift and a child whose shraddha won't let it pass.
what a scholar hears: the Katha expands a shorter Nachiketas story in the Taittiriya Brahmana (3.11.8), where the father's words are also 'to Death I give you'.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1.1–1.1.6 (the sacrifice, the cows, 'to whom will you give me?')

notes: Katha 1.1.1–1.1.6 paraphrased; the father is also called Auddalaki Aruni / Gautama in 1.1.11 — kept to Vajashravasa.
Nachiketa's name etymology ('one who does not know') is traditional and uncertain; check or drop.
